section.title: The Faithful Have Vanished
section.sectionRationale: A lament over a society flooded with flattery and lies, in which the LORD's own promised rising for the oppressed and His flawless, refined words stand as the one sure thing in a world where the faithful seem to have vanished.
section.thesis: When the godly have vanished and flattering, double-hearted lies fill every mouth, the LORD promises to arise for the oppressed, and His own words, unlike human words, are flawless, refined like silver seven times in the fire.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the cry that the faithful have vanished amid flattering lips (vv1-2), a plea for the LORD to cut off proud tongues (vv3-4), the LORD's own promise to arise for the oppressed (v5), and the closing confidence in His flawless word amid a world where vileness is exalted (vv6-8).

units.label: The faithful have vanished
units.note: flattering lips and a double heart

verses.text: Help, O LORD, for the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men.
They lie to one another; they speak with flattering lips and a double heart.
May the LORD cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue.
They say, "With our tongues we will prevail. We own our lips, who can be our master?"
"For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise," says the LORD. "I will bring safety to him who yearns."

units.label: Flawless words in a vile world

verses.text: The words of the LORD are {{tzaruf|flawless}}, like silver refined in a furnace, like gold purified sevenfold.
You, O LORD, will keep us; You will forever guard us from this generation.
The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men.

tzaruf.gloss: Refined, purified, tested by fire until every impurity is removed. The LORD's words are described this way, flawless like silver refined seven times, an image of total trustworthiness set directly against the deceitful, double-hearted human speech that fills the rest of the psalm.

basic.context: Psalm 12 is a cry over a society where the godly seem to have vanished, replaced by flattering lips and double hearts, and where proud tongues boast that they answer to no one. Against this flood of deceit, the LORD speaks His own promise to arise for the oppressed, and His words are declared flawless, unlike the lies filling every mouth around David.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm names social and moral decay honestly, the godly vanishing, deceit becoming normal, without despairing, because the psalm's center of gravity shifts from human unreliability to the flawless reliability of God's own word; the contrast between corrupt human speech and God's refined speech is the psalm's whole argument.
basic.originalLanguages: The proud boast, 'with our tongues we will prevail, we own our lips, who can be our master,' asserting total independence from any authority over their speech. Against this, God's words are tzaruf, refined or purified, an image of silver tested by fire until every impurity is gone, purified sevenfold, a number signifying completeness.
basic.typology: The LORD's own spoken promise to arise for the oppressed and needy, set directly against the deceit of human speech, anticipates Christ, the Word made flesh, whose speech, unlike fallen human words, is perfectly trustworthy and who Himself arose for the oppressed.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Word of God in person, John 1:1, the flawless speech this psalm celebrates now embodied; where human words fail and flatter, His word never passes away, Matthew 24:35, and He is the one who has already arisen, in the resurrection, for the cause of the oppressed and needy.
basic.god: God is not merely one truthful voice among many competing voices; He is the standard against which all other speech is measured, His words tested and proven flawless, and He personally intervenes, arising for the sake of the groaning needy rather than remaining a distant observer of deceit.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 18:30 similarly declares the LORD's word flawless. John 1:1-14 identifies Jesus as the Word made flesh. James 3:5-10 laments the tongue's capacity for deceit and inconsistency, echoing this psalm's concern.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 12 names a world flooded with flattery and lies and answers it not with a clever human strategy but with God's own flawless word and His personal promise to arise for the oppressed, a promise embodied fully in Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh who arose indeed.

context.literary:
Psalm 12 is a psalm about words, and it is built out of them. The vocabulary of speech saturates its eight verses: lips, tongues, lying, flattering, boasting, saying, words. It is a small, tightly made poem, and the structure is easy to see once the speakers are marked. In verses 1 and 2 the psalmist speaks in a cry, in verses 3 and 4 he prays and quotes the wicked, in verse 5 the LORD speaks in the first person, in verses 6 and 7 the psalmist answers the LORD's speech with a meditation and a confession, and in verse 8 the poem ends with the world as it still is.

The core of the poem is a contrast between two kinds of speech. Human mouths in verses 2 to 4 are lips that lie, that flatter, and that boast of their own mastery. God's mouth in verse 5 is a promise, and in verse 6 the psalmist says that promise, and by extension every word of the LORD, is like silver refined in a furnace. The refining language answers the corruption of human talk. One kind of speech is alloyed and the other is pure.

There is a symmetry in the framing. The psalm begins with a cry for help, and the verb for help in verse 1 is the same root as the 'safety' promised in verse 5, so the request and the LORD's reply are the same word. In verse 1 the psalmist says the faithful have vanished, and in verse 7 he says the LORD will keep them. The psalm ends, however, not on a note of arrival but with verse 8, 'The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men.' The final line does not cancel the promise. It leaves the tension in place, as if the poet were unwilling to pretend that hearing God's word had emptied the streets of liars.
context.historical:
The heading in the Hebrew, 'according to the Sheminith,' uses a word that also appears in the headings of Psalm 6 and in 1 Chronicles 15:21, and the BSB footnote calls it probably a musical term. It is generally taken to be an instruction for the choirmaster and is not tied to a setting. The psalm carries David's name in its Hebrew heading, and its picture of a court or city in which honesty has collapsed fits the years when he lived under Saul's suspicion, or, as some prefer, the period of intrigue in his own household and kingdom later.

The world behind the poem is one in which speech was social currency. In a society without written contracts for most dealings, an oath, a promise, a testimony at the town gate carried the weight of law. A flatterer with a 'double heart,' literally 'a heart and a heart,' was a man who said one thing and meant another, the kind of witness who could destroy a neighbour in court. The prophets record the same erosion in Israel's later life, Micah 7:2 and Isaiah 59:4. When the psalmist says the faithful have 'vanished,' he is describing the loss of that reliable speech.

The wicked's boast, 'We own our lips, who can be our master?' is a claim of the powerful in a culture in which kings and elites could say what they liked and could not be held to account. It declares that speech is a private possession, that no law or God has a claim on it. The claim runs against the covenant, where the ninth commandment forbids false testimony, Exodus 20:16.

The imagery of silver refined in a furnace was familiar to a people who lived among metalworkers. Silver was purified by heating until the dross rose and was skimmed off, and 'sevenfold' means completely, as seven was the number of fullness. The psalm places the LORD's word in the assayer's fire, where nothing has been left in it that could fail.
context.canonical:
Psalm 12 sits among the psalms of Book One that deal with slander and with deception, Psalm 5:9, 10:7, 28:3, 31:18 and 120:2. Together they form a subject in the Psalter: the tongue as a weapon. Psalm 55:21 has the same double heart, 'His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart.' What Psalm 12 adds is the counterpart. Against the many verses of complaint about human words it sets the assurance of divine ones.

Its central image, the refined word, gathers up a stream of Scripture. Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31 say the word of the LORD is flawless, Proverbs 30:5 says every word of God is flawless and that He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him, and Psalm 119:140 says His promise is completely pure. All use the same refining vocabulary, and Psalm 119, the long psalm in praise of God's word, unfolds what Psalm 12 states in one line.

The oracle of verse 5, 'now I will arise,' has a close parallel in Isaiah 33:10, where the LORD says three times 'Now I will arise... now I will lift Myself up... now I will be exalted,' at the moment when human plans have failed. The LORD's rising is the Old Testament's response to the failure of every human helper, Isaiah 59:16.

In the New Testament, the psalm's concerns are taken up in the teaching on speech. Jesus says the mouth speaks from the overflow of the heart, Matthew 12:34, and asks for a plain yes and a plain no, Matthew 5:37. James says no man can tame the tongue, James 3:8, and Paul tells believers to put off falsehood and speak truthfully, Ephesians 4:25. And it is in the Gospel of John that God's word takes flesh: 'Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth,' John 17:17, and the Word became flesh, John 1:14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted his hearers to know what to do when the culture around them stops telling the truth. The psalm begins with the sense of isolation that many faithful people feel, that the godly have gone and only liars remain. It is a cry a whole assembly could say, and it validates the experience. The first thing the psalm gives is permission to say plainly that the situation is bad.

He also intended to show that the problem is not just manners but a claim of sovereignty. The wicked do not merely lie, they say, 'We own our lips.' That is a statement about who is the master. The psalmist wants Israel to see that a society of flatterers and boasters has in fact set itself up as a rival to God, and that the question 'who can be our master?' has an answer.

The heart of the psalm's teaching is the shift in verse 5. The LORD says He will arise because of the groaning of the needy, so that the psalm turns not on what the faithful do but on what God says. The hearers are meant to notice that the remedy for a world of unreliable words is a reliable word, and that the reliable word has come from outside the human situation. Faith is placed on speech that has been tested.

And he meant the closing verse to keep the hearers honest. Verse 8 refuses an easy resolution. The believer is to hold the promise in one hand and the world as it is in the other, keeping both. The psalm trains the community to wait on God's word while the wicked still strut.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes the speech of the wicked, their flattery, their double hearts, their boast, and it describes God's promise. It does not tell the reader to imitate the first or to expect the second on demand. The wicked's boast is quoted so that it can be refuted, not adopted.

What the psalm implies for conduct is worth drawing out carefully. The faithful person is one who does not lie to his neighbour and does not flatter, and the psalm's disgust at 'flattering lips' and a 'double heart' is a standard for the listener, echoed in James 3:9 and 10 and Ephesians 4:25. Yet the psalm does not hand the worshipper a programme for reforming a corrupt society by his own effort. The action it prescribes is prayer, 'Help, O LORD,' and reliance on God's speech.

There is also a caution about the promise in verse 5. It is spoken to the needy who groan, and it is a promise that God will act. It is not a guarantee that a particular believer's particular problem will be resolved in the manner or the time he expects. The psalm ends with the wicked still walking about, so it does not describe a formula in which trust in God's word removes every liar from view. The word is to be trusted precisely because the circumstances do not yet match it.

debates.question: Whose words are described as flawless and refined in verse 6, human vows of protection or God's own promise in verse 5?

views.label: God's words specifically, His promise in verse 5
views.case: The verse immediately follows the LORD's direct speech in verse 5, so the flawless words most naturally refer to God's own trustworthy promise to arise for the oppressed, contrasted with the untrustworthy words of the wicked throughout the psalm.

views.label: God's words in general, His whole revealed speech
views.case: The image of refined silver fits a broader biblical pattern, echoed in Psalm 18:30 and Psalm 19:7-9, celebrating the trustworthiness of God's revealed word as a whole, not only the specific promise of verse 5.

debates.bearing: Either reading reaches the same pastoral conclusion: in a world of flattering, deceitful human speech, God's own word, whether His specific promise or His whole revelation, stands utterly reliable and worth staking one's life on.

debates.question: How does the LORD's word in verse 5 reach the psalmist?

views.label: An oracle delivered in worship
views.case: The abrupt shift to the LORD speaking in the first person looks like the oracle that a priest or prophet delivered in the temple in response to a lament. Other psalms have the same shape, a complaint followed by a divine word, and the psalm's reply in verse 6 sounds like a congregation's response to what was just heard.

views.label: An inward assurance given in prayer
views.case: Some see the quotation as the psalmist's own confidence, given by God in the course of prayer, and set down as if spoken. The psalm gives no sign of a second speaker, and the verb 'says the LORD' can be taken as the psalmist's report of what he has come to know.

views.label: A recollection of what God had already promised in Scripture
views.case: The LORD's concern for the groaning needy echoes the law, in which God promises to hear the cry of the widow and orphan, Exodus 22:23. On this reading the psalmist reminds himself of the standing word of the LORD and applies it to his day.

debates.bearing: The three readings do not change what the psalm asks of its readers. In each, the psalmist is held by a word from God that stands outside his own circumstances, and the community is invited to lean on it. Whether spoken by a priest, breathed in prayer, or recalled from the law, the word is treated as trustworthy because of who speaks it.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm opens with 'Help,' hoshia, the imperative of the root that also means to save, and it comes back in the promise of verse 5, where the LORD says He will bring 'safety,' from the noun yesha, of the same root. The psalm's beginning and its promise share one word family, so what the psalmist asks for is what God promises to give. Salvation in this sense is rescue from the people whose words crush.

The 'godly' of verse 1 are the chasid, the man of covenant loyalty, from chesed, and the 'faithful' are emunim, from the root aman, the root of 'amen,' meaning firm, reliable, trustworthy. The lament is that both types have gone, the loyal and the reliable, and the vocabulary already tells the reader what is lacking: people whose word can bear weight.

Verse 2 says they speak 'lies,' and the Hebrew is shav, which means emptiness, nothingness, something with no substance. The same word appears in the third commandment, 'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain,' Exodus 20:7, and in the ninth, false witness. Their talk is hollow. The flatterers have 'smooth lips,' the sense of the Hebrew, slippery, and they speak 'with a heart and a heart,' which is how the Hebrew says double heart. It is a compact and vivid phrase: one heart for the face and another for the truth.

The boast of verse 4 uses the noun adon, 'lord, master,' in the question 'who is master over us?' It is the word Israel used of a human superior and, in its plural or emphatic forms, of God Himself. The wicked ask who can be their adon, and the psalm's answer is the LORD, whom the verse 6 introduces by name, and in verse 1 and 5 the same divine name that the wicked ignore.

In verse 5 the LORD's own announcement begins with 'Now,' atta, 'now I will arise.' The little word matters. It marks the point at which the LORD's patience turns to action, and Isaiah 33:10 uses the same construction three times. It is an oracle, a word in the first person from God, and it is delivered as a decision.

Verse 6 contrasts the LORD's words with the human words of verses 2 to 4. The Hebrew for 'words' is imrot, and the adjective is tehorot, 'pure, clean,' a word used of ritual cleanliness, so the words are as clean as sacrificial vessels. Then the image of silver refined in a furnace uses the participle tsaruf, refined, the same word as Psalm 18:30. The BSB footnote to verse 6 says the phrase is a 'probable reading,' and that the received Hebrew text has 'like silver refined in a furnace of clay,' a phrase that is hard to parse. Whatever the exact picture, the point stands. The last word, 'sevenfold,' is a dual form in Hebrew, best taken as 'twice seven times over,' the language of totality.

typology.type: The refined word of the LORD, Psalm 12:6
typology.fulfillment: The psalm sets the pure words of God against the alloyed talk of men. In the New Testament that word has a face. 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and Jesus says of His words, 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away,' Matthew 24:35. Peter says of Him, 'He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22. The correspondence is real, the flawless speech of God spoken in a human mouth. The type falls short in that the psalm speaks of words that promise, while Christ is the promise made flesh, 2 Corinthians 1:20.

typology.type: The LORD who arises for the groaning needy, Psalm 12:5
typology.fulfillment: The LORD promises to rise for the oppressed. The gospel says He did, in person. Luke opens with Zechariah's song, 'the Dawn will visit us from on high,' Luke 1:78, and Jesus declares that He has come to bring good news to the poor, Luke 4:18. God's rising is finally the resurrection, when the crucified one, condemned by false witnesses, was raised. Matthew records that many false witnesses came forward against Him, Matthew 26:59 and 60. The pattern is not exhausted, since the psalm is still prayed in a world where the needy still groan.

typology.type: The silver refined in a furnace, Psalm 12:6
typology.fulfillment: The refining image describes God's word, and the Old Testament also uses it of God's people, Zechariah 13:9 and Psalm 66:10. The New Testament applies it to faith tested by trial, 1 Peter 1:7, where faith proved genuine is worth more than gold refined by fire. There is a pattern in the correspondence: the pure word makes a pure people. But the furnace also falls on Christ. He is the one 'tested in every way' yet without sin, Hebrews 4:15, so the refining that produced flawless speech in Him is the pattern for what the Spirit produces in believers. The image should not be pressed into an allegory of each stage of refining.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first through the contrast between two kinds of speech, and that contrast reaches its climax in Jesus. The wicked in the psalm are men of flattery and a double heart, with lips that say one thing while the heart means another. Jesus is described as the one in whose mouth 'no deceit was found,' 1 Peter 2:22, and He can say, 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. Before Pilate He says, 'For this reason I was born and have come into the world, to testify to the truth,' John 18:37. In a world where men claimed to own their lips, He gave His words to the Father and said that He spoke what the Father gave Him. The Amen, the faithful and true Witness, is His title in Revelation 3:14, and the rider on the white horse is called 'Faithful and True,' Revelation 19:11.

It leads to Christ by the promise of the LORD's rising. In verse 5 God says He will arise for the needy. When the Gospels tell the story of Jesus they tell of one who came among the poor, healed the sick, and pronounced good news for the oppressed. Even His trial fits the psalm. He was accused by false witnesses, whose lips were smooth and whose hearts were double, Matthew 26:59 and 60, and He was condemned by the words of those who boasted they had no king but Caesar, John 19:15. The God who arises did so in the resurrection, and Peter's words at Pentecost that God raised Him up, Acts 2:24, are the answer to the psalm's 'Now I will arise.'

It leads to Christ through the flawless word that stands. Isaiah says the word of our God stands forever, Isaiah 40:8, and Peter quotes it and applies it to the gospel, 1 Peter 1:25. In Christ the word is not only reliable but present, so that trusting His word is trusting the person. John records His prayer, 'Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth,' John 17:17, and His promise, 'If you continue in My word, you are truly My disciples. Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free,' John 8:31 and 32.

The psalm also leads to Christ in the sense of the guarded remnant. 'You, O LORD, will keep us.' Jesus prays to the Father to keep those given to Him, John 17:11, and His own words promise that no one can snatch them from His hand, John 10:28. The faithful who had vanished are gathered in Him.

A caution belongs here. Psalm 12 does not predict a Messiah by name, and its contrast is between the human speech of David's day and God's reliable word. The claim that Jesus is the flawless Word rests on the New Testament's own identification of Him as the Word and on its use of the psalm's themes, not on reading Him into each line.
study.god:
Psalm 12 shows a God who speaks and whose speech can bear any weight. This is the first thing the psalm says about Him. In a world where words are unreliable, the LORD's words are refined silver. The Bible teaches elsewhere that God 'is not a man, that He should lie,' Numbers 23:19, and that He 'cannot lie,' Titus 1:2. Truthfulness is not a virtue He has but who He is. That is why His promises are the anchor the psalmist grasps when the faithful have vanished.

God hears the groaning of the needy. The psalm says that the reason God will arise is the cause of the oppressed and the groaning of the needy, verse 5. His action is not prompted by a change in the world's morality or by human petition alone, but by the sound of suffering. The word groaning is wordless, and this is a God who responds to inarticulate pain as well as to formulated prayer. The needy do not have to speak well to be heard.

He is a personal agent who intervenes. The psalm does not describe a principle that will eventually correct itself. It says, 'I will now arise,' first person. The doctrine of providence here is not impersonal. There is a Someone who chooses to act, who has waited until now, and who gives His word about what He will do. That word is spoken to those who have no strength to make it happen.

He is a keeper. 'You, O LORD, will keep us; You will forever guard us,' verse 7. The two verbs, keep and guard, are the language of a shepherd or a watchman. The psalm's vision of God is not only of the one who arises to punish but of the one who stays with His people through the whole span of a hostile generation.

He alone is the master. The wicked ask who can be their master. The psalm lets the question stand in the air and then answers it with the entire structure of the poem. The claim that one has no lord over one's own lips is a claim against God, and the God of the psalm is shown to have the last word, in every sense.

Yet He is patient with a hard tension. Verse 8 leaves the wicked walking about. The God of the psalm is shown as one who has spoken and will act, and who has not yet acted. The psalm asks for trust in a word rather than a sight.

For worship, this means that the primary act of faith in a world of lies is listening. To worship the God of this psalm is to take His word as the fixed point when everything else has become unreliable, and to speak in prayer as one who has been spoken to first. It also means to be a person whose own words are reliable, because a people who trust a truthful God should not become flatterers.

crossReferences.note: The word of the LORD is flawless, and He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him. It uses the same refining vocabulary as Psalm 12:6. David appears to say in his victory song what the writer here says in his lament, so that the flawless word is a truth both in triumph and in distress.

Every word of God is flawless, and He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him. It widens the psalm's claim from the promise of verse 5 to all of God's speech, and adds the practical consequence, that those who rely on the word find it a place of shelter.

Your promise is completely pure; therefore Your servant loves it. It voices the response the psalm invites, love for a word that has been tested. It also shows that the vocabulary of purity applied to God's word became the regular language of the Psalter's meditation on Scripture.

The LORD says 'Now I will arise,' three times over, when human power has been exposed as empty. It repeats the announcement of Psalm 12:5 in a national crisis, and it shows that the promise that God will rise is a stable pattern in Israel's story, not a one off.

His speech is smooth as butter but war is in his heart, and his words are softer than oil yet they are swords unsheathed. It is a longer portrait of the double heart of Psalm 12:2, showing what lies behind flattery, a hidden aggression that uses gentle words as a weapon.

The godly man has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among men. It nearly repeats Psalm 12:1 two centuries later, showing that the sense of a vanished faithful remnant recurs, and that the prophets and psalmists faced it with the same recourse to God.

Out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks. Jesus supplies the diagnosis behind the psalm's double heart. The problem of flattering lips is a problem of the heart, and the remedy must reach as deep, which is why the psalm looks beyond human effort.

No man can tame the tongue, a restless evil full of deadly poison. It echoes the psalm's alarm about tongues that claim to prevail, and it concludes as the psalm does, that the cure has to come from God, not from human resolve.

God is not a man that He should lie. It gives the theology behind the contrast in Psalm 12 between human and divine words. Balaam is forced to say that what the LORD has spoken He will do, which is the confidence the psalmist rests on in verses 5 and 6.

Jesus prays that the Father sanctify His people by the truth, and says the Father's word is truth. It takes the psalm's claim about the purity of God's words and makes it the medium of holiness, so that to be set apart is to be shaped by the flawless word.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 12 goes back to the beginning of the Bible's story, where the first lie was spoken. The serpent's question 'Did God really say?' in Genesis 3:1 set the pattern: human speech turned against God's, flattery in place of truth. The psalm's picture of a generation of lying lips is the long aftermath. Jesus calls the devil the father of lies, John 8:44, and Psalm 12 sketches what a world formed by that father looks like when it becomes a culture.

The story then follows how God answered. He did not answer with a set of ideas but with a word spoken and kept. To Abraham He spoke a promise and confirmed it by an oath, since He could swear by no one greater, Hebrews 6:13 and 14. To Israel He spoke at Sinai, and the covenant was made in words. When Israel's own leaders fell into the flattery and corruption the psalm describes, prophet after prophet came with a word from the LORD, and the pattern of Psalm 12:5, God speaking when human speech fails, is repeated through the whole story.

The story then comes to its centre in Christ, who is the Word of God in person. In Him God's flawless speech does not merely accompany deliverance, it is the deliverer. He is the one who spoke and it was done, who calmed storms with a word, and whose death was accompanied by false witness, and who rose. The church that lives by His word lives by the psalm, in a world where people still say 'We own our lips.'

The story ends where the psalm hopes. In the new heaven and new earth no falsehood will enter, Revelation 21:27, and the ones outside are those who love and practise lying, Revelation 22:15. The needy will no longer groan. The faithful who had vanished will be found in a great company, and the words of the LORD, which were flawless from the start, will be seen to have been true in every syllable. The last line of the psalm, in which vileness is exalted, will belong forever to the past, and what God promised in verse 5, safety for him who yearns, will be the condition of everyone in His city.

quiz.q: What is David's opening complaint in Psalm 12:1-2?

options.text: That the godly and faithful have vanished, replaced by flattering lips and a double heart.
options.note: This is the psalm's specific opening lament over widespread social and moral decay.

options.text: That he has lost a specific battle.
options.note: The complaint concerns pervasive deceit and the vanishing of the godly, not a specific military defeat.

options.text: That he is suffering a physical illness.
options.note: The complaint is about deceitful speech and social decay, not physical sickness.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm opens in praise.
options.note: Verses 1-2 open with an urgent complaint, not praise.

quiz.q: What do the proud boast about their own speech in verse 4?

options.text: That they will prevail with their tongues and answer to no master over their own lips.
options.note: This boast asserts total independence from any authority over their speech.

options.text: That they will submit fully to God's authority.
options.note: The boast is the opposite, a claim of independence from any master, including God.

options.text: That they intend to speak only truth from now on.
options.note: The boast is about asserting freedom to speak as they please, not a commitment to truthfulness.

options.text: Nothing is quoted from the proud in this psalm.
options.note: Verse 4 directly quotes their boastful claim about their own tongues and lips.

quiz.q: What does the LORD Himself promise in verse 5?

options.text: That He will now arise for the cause of the oppressed and needy and bring safety to the one who yearns.
options.note: This direct divine speech is the psalm's turning point, God's personal promise to act.

options.text: That He will remain passive and uninvolved.
options.note: This is the opposite of what verse 5 states; God promises active intervention.

options.text: That He will destroy Israel for its unfaithfulness.
options.note: The promise is to act for the oppressed and needy, not a threat against Israel as a whole.

options.text: Nothing is spoken by the LORD in this psalm.
options.note: Verse 5 contains a direct, first-person promise spoken by the LORD Himself.

quiz.q: How are the LORD's words described in verse 6?

options.text: Flawless, like silver refined in a furnace and purified sevenfold.
options.note: This image of tested, purified metal describes the total trustworthiness of God's words.

options.text: Uncertain and open to later revision.
options.note: The image of refined silver conveys total reliability, not uncertainty or the need for revision.

options.text: Similar in reliability to human promises.
options.note: The psalm draws a sharp contrast between God's flawless words and unreliable human speech, not a similarity.

options.text: The psalm gives no description of God's words.
options.note: Verse 6 gives an explicit, vivid description of God's flawless, refined words.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's contrast between human speech and God's word connect to Jesus?

options.text: Jesus is the Word made flesh, whose word never passes away, embodying the flawless speech this psalm celebrates and fulfilling God's promise to arise for the oppressed through His resurrection.
options.note: John 1:14 and Matthew 24:35 connect directly to this psalm's themes of God's trustworthy word and promised rising.

options.text: This psalm has no connection to Jesus or the New Testament.
options.note: The psalm's themes of God's flawless word and promised rising connect meaningfully to Christ as the Word made flesh who rose from the dead.

options.text: It only describes ancient Israelite social customs with no lasting significance.
options.note: The psalm's contrast between corrupt speech and God's flawless word carries forward meaningfully into the New Testament's picture of Christ.

options.text: It predicts the exact wording of the Gospel of John.
options.note: The connection is thematic and typological, not a specific verbal prediction.

questions: David laments that the godly seem to have vanished and flattery and lies fill every mouth. Where do you see this same pattern in your own culture or community today, and how do you respond to it without despair?

The proud boast that their tongues are their own and answer to no master. Where might you be tempted to speak carelessly, as though your words answer to no one, rather than remembering they are heard by God?

God speaks directly in this psalm, promising to arise for the oppressed and needy. What situation of oppression or need are you currently waiting for God to act on, and how does His direct promise here encourage your waiting?

God's words are described as flawless, tested like refined silver, unlike the corrupt speech surrounding David. How does trusting the reliability of Scripture change the way you face a world full of half-truths and flattery?

The psalm ends acknowledging that the wicked still wander freely and vileness is still exalted, even after God's promise. How do you hold together confidence in God's word with the reality that evil often still seems to prosper for a time?

translationNotes.note: Upon the Sheminith, meaning the eighth, likely names an instrument, a lower vocal register, or an eight-stringed instrument, appearing also in the superscription of Psalm 6; its exact meaning is uncertain today.
In 'our lips, who can be our master', the proud claim total ownership of their own speech.

Purified sevenfold pictures repeated refining of silver in a furnace until every impurity is removed, the number seven signifying completeness, an image of the total, perfect reliability of God's words.
